To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dentate gyrusexhibits a unique form of network oscillation that is composed of a slow theta and a faster gamma oscillation.
theta-gamma oscillations are a key reference signal in the hippocampus for information processing, and that these network oscillations are mediated by theta-gamma-modulation of synaptic inputs.

theta-gamma oscillations in the dentate network are driven by barrages of theta-modulated excitatory and gamma-modulated inhibitory synaptic currents in GCs in vivo, and these oscillations are associated with sparse firing of GCs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synaptic mechanisms of theta-gamma network oscillation in the hippocampus.
the role of network oscillations for information processing in the dentate granule cell layer.
the synaptic and cellular basis of network oscillations and their role in information processing in neuronal networks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
theta-gamma oscillations are generated by the interaction between the hippocampus, entorhinal and perirhinal cortex, as well as the medial septum and the thalamus.
the theta-gamma-modulation of synaptic currents is an important mechanism for information processing in the dentate granule cells in vivo.
theta-gamma-modulation of synaptic currents in GCs provides a mechanism for network oscillations in the dentate.

we have shown that theta-gamma-modulation of synaptic currents in the granule cell layer of the dentate gyrum in vivo provides a framework for sparse, temporal coding of information.

The main takeaway from our work is that

theta and gamma oscillations are not only observed as network activity, but they also modulate synaptic currents in individual neurons, and thus may be important for information processing in the brain.
